name: Danish
intro: Danish spelling substantially underrepresents its spoken sound patterns. Vowel distinctions, reduction, soft d and stød require sustained listening with a specific model. Standard written Danish is the principal model. Do not attempt to derive an accent solely from a word's spelling or from Norwegian and Swedish similarities.

foundation.name: Danish
notes: Æ, Ø and Å come after Z in that order. They are distinct letters. aa sometimes remains in names and older spellings for å. Letter names are for spelling; spelling alone does not reliably predict the spoken vowel.

Danish has a large vowel inventory, reductions and the soft d, which is not an ordinary English d. Stød is a laryngeal feature in many words, not simply stress. Learn it from a clear recording and imitation rather than an English respelling.
An ending may be weakly pronounced while still carrying a grammatical distinction. Learn en/et with each noun and listen to singular/plural and indefinite/definite pairs.
building: en bog → bogen = a book → the book; et hus → huset = a house → the house. With an adjective: den gode bog = the good book.
en stor bil, et stort hus, store huse = a large car, a large house, large houses. Many adjectives show common-gender, neuter and plural forms, but exceptions must be learned.
arbejde + plads → arbejdsplads = workplace. Linking -s- is lexical; do not insert it in every compound.

sections.title: Nouns and adjective agreement
sections.explanation: Danish has common-gender en and neuter et nouns, with suffixed definite forms: en bog/bogen, et hus/huset. Plural patterns are lexical. Adjectives commonly use -t in neuter singular and -e in plural or definite phrases. Standard definite adjective phrases use a separate determiner with a normally non-suffixed noun: det store hus, unlike the typical Swedish double-definite construction.
examples: et nyt forslag / det nye forslag
a new proposal / the new proposal
exercises: Choose det store hus or det store huset in the core standard Danish pattern.
Det store hus. The separate definite determiner accompanies the adjective and unsuffixed noun.
What must a noun card preserve?
En/et, definite and plural forms, pronunciation and usage.

sections.title: Verb-second and subordinate negation
sections.explanation: Main declaratives use verb-second: I dag læser jeg rapporten. In subordinate clauses, ikke commonly precedes the finite verb: fordi jeg ikke ved. Main-clause ikke commonly follows the finite verb. Clause boundaries determine the pattern; a long initial constituent does not license English word order afterward.
examples: Jeg ved, at hun ikke kommer.
I know that she is not coming.
exercises: Reorder i morgen / vi / mødes.
I morgen mødes vi.
Place ikke after fordi in fordi han ved det.
Fordi han ikke ved det.

sections.title: Tense, passive and modal meanings
sections.explanation: Verbs normally do not vary by person. Perfect uses an auxiliary and participle; learn har/er choices in actual verbs. The -s passive and blive + participle are common passive strategies with lexical and register differences. Må can express permission in many contexts and should not be mechanically equated with Norwegian må. Skal, bør and behøver express different obligation or necessity meanings.
examples: You do not need to wait.
exercises: Why is transferring a cognate modal from Norwegian risky?
Similar forms can have different conventional meanings; Danish må often concerns permission.
Ask May I ask a question?
Må jeg stille et spørgsmål? Permission question.

sections.title: Relatives, possession and discourse
sections.explanation: Som and der occur in relative structures with distributional differences, including subject-relative contexts. Sin/sit/sine refer reflexively to an appropriate singular subject in core patterns; hans/hendes are nonreflexive. The possessed noun selects the form. Derfor expresses consequence, derimod contrast and alligevel concession.
examples: Det er metoden, som vi bruger.
It is the method we use.
exercises: Choose sin/sit with forslag.
Sit forslag, since forslag is neuter.
Write a concession with alligevel.
Resultaterne er interessante. Alligevel har vi brug for flere oplysninger.

sections.title: Professional reading
sections.explanation:
Teaching passage: Resultaterne viser en sammenhæng mellem to faktorer. De beviser dog ikke, at den ene faktor forårsager den anden. Undersøgelsens betingelser skal indgå i vurderingen.
Translation: The results show an association between two factors. However, they do not prove that one causes the other. The study conditions must be included in the assessment.
examples: Could you elaborate on this point?
exercises: Summarise the reasoning.
Association is shown, causal proof is denied and study conditions must be assessed.
Record a short summary after reading.
Use a real Danish model for vowels, reduction and stød; the book supplies the content, not the acoustic model.

rules.title: En and et nouns
rules.explanation: Danish has common and neuter grammatical gender. En/et is part of a noun’s lexical information. Definite singular often adds -en/-et directly to the noun.

examples.native: "Oh, var jeg dog sådant et stort træ, som de andre!" sukkede det lille grantræ.
examples.translation: "Oh, if I were only as great a tree as the others!" sighed the little Fir.

examples.native: Marathi er navnet på et vigtigt indoarisk sprog, der tales i det vestlige og centrale Indien.
examples.translation: Marathi is the name of an important Indo-Aryan language spoken in western and central India.

examples.native: Dette er en offentlig gade, ikke en væddeløbsbane!
examples.translation: This is a public street, not a racetrack.

rules.title: Definite and demonstrative forms
rules.explanation: Den/det/de precede many definite adjective phrases and can serve as pronouns. Their form depends on gender/number. Context distinguishes article and demonstrative functions.

examples.native: Bærer din kone det muslimske tørklæde?
examples.translation: Does your wife wear the Muslim headscarf?

examples.native: Gør bare det færdigt som du er i gang med.
examples.translation: Just finish what you're doing.

examples.native: Hvor er det koldt!
examples.translation: How cold it is!

rules.title: Personal pronouns
rules.explanation: Subject and object pronoun forms differ. Danish finite verbs generally do not change for person. Capital I means plural you and differs from lowercase i, in.

examples.native: Vi kender ham ikke.
examples.translation: We don't know him.

examples.native: Tom havde al ret til at gøre, hvad han gjorde.
examples.translation: Tom had every right to do what he did.

examples.native: Jeg ville gøre alt for dig.
examples.translation: I'd do anything for you.

rules.title: Copula and past
rules.explanation: Er is a present form for all persons; var is past; været is the participle. Subject changes do not create English-style am/is/are variation.

examples.native: Mørke er fravær af lys.
examples.translation: Darkness is the absence of light.

examples.native: At fejle er menneskeligt, at tilgive er guddommeligt.
examples.translation: To err is human; to forgive, divine.

examples.native: Dette er deres hus.
examples.translation: This is their house.

rules.title: Have forms
rules.explanation: Har expresses present possession or serves as an auxiliary; havde is past and haft a participle. Learn a perfect together with its auxiliary and intended meaning.

examples.native: Hun har blondt hår.
examples.translation: She has blonde hair.

examples.native: Alle havde meget travlt.
examples.translation: Everybody was very busy.

examples.native: Kunden har ikke altid ret.
examples.translation: The customer isn't always right.

rules.title: Main-clause negation
rules.explanation: In many ordinary main statements the finite verb precedes ikke. In a subordinate clause, sentence adverbs often precede the finite verb. The connector and clause status determine the pattern.

examples.native: Tom kan endnu ikke køre bil.
examples.translation: Tom can't drive a car yet.

examples.native: Tom drak ikke noget.
examples.translation: Tom didn't drink anything.

examples.native: Lyt ikke til dem.
examples.translation: Don't listen to them.

rules.title: Subordinate connectors
rules.explanation: These connectors commonly introduce subordinate structures. Compare Jeg kommer ikke with fordi jeg ikke kommer. Main-clause verb-second order counts constituents, not words.

examples.native: Hun nægtede at skrive under på andragendet.
examples.translation: She refused to sign the petition.

examples.native: Sami forsøgte at sælge sin bil.
examples.translation: Sami tried to sell his car.

examples.native: Jeg antog at hun var din kæreste.
examples.translation: I assumed she was your girlfriend.

rules.title: Coordination
rules.explanation: Coordinating connectors link phrases or clauses. For can function as a causal conjunction or as a preposition; analyse the following structure.

examples.native: Tak for indsatsen.
examples.translation: Thanks for the effort.

examples.native: Han så til højre og gik.
examples.translation: He looked right and left.

examples.native: Min bror taler for meget.
examples.translation: My brother talks too much.

rules.title: Modals
rules.explanation: Modals express ability, duty, permission, prediction or intention. They normally combine with a bare infinitive. Their past forms can also create polite or hypothetical distance.

examples.native: Tom vil lære serbisk.
examples.translation: Tom wants to learn Serbian.

examples.native: Tom ville sælge sin bil.
examples.translation: Tom wanted to sell his car.

examples.native: Dit ønske vil gå i opfyldelse i nær fremtid.
examples.translation: Your wish will come true in the near future.

rules.title: Perfect participles
rules.explanation: A perfect combines har or er with a participle. Auxiliary choice can depend on the verb and meaning. A participle may also appear in a passive or as an adjective.

examples.native: Jeg har set dig gøre det.
examples.translation: I've seen you doing that.

examples.native: Hun er ikke kommet.
examples.translation: She did not come.

examples.native: Tom har sagt at han er bange for at hans telefon er klogere end han er.
examples.translation: Tom said that he's scared that his phone is smarter than he is.

rules.title: Past lexical verbs
rules.explanation: Common strong verbs have irregular past forms. Practice the subject and time frame with the form; Danish verbs do not normally conjugate for person.

examples.native: Undskyld, noget gik galt.
examples.translation: Sorry, something went wrong.

examples.native: Alt gik op i røg.
examples.translation: Everything went up in smoke.

examples.native: Jeg sagde til min kone: Liliane, pak kufferterne, vi tager tilbage til Paris.
examples.translation: I told my wife: Liliane, pack up the bags, we're going back to Paris.

rules.title: Adjective agreement
rules.explanation: Adjectives often distinguish common singular, neuter singular and plural/definite forms. Lille has irregular plural små. Predicative adjectives also show relevant agreement.

examples.native: Jeg trænger til en ny cykel.
examples.translation: I need a new bicycle.

examples.native: Han kan virkelig godt lide at rejse.
examples.translation: He really likes traveling a lot.

examples.native: Jeg er ikke ret god til at lave mad; derfor spiser jeg tit ude.
examples.translation: I'm not very good at cooking, so I eat out a lot.

rules.title: Reflexive possession
rules.explanation: Sin/sit/sine refers back to a third-person subject in suitable contexts. Hans/hendes can refer to somebody else. Reflexive possession does not simply mean any English his/her.

examples.native: Tom fodrer sin hund to gange om dagen.
examples.translation: Tom feeds his dog twice a day.

examples.native: De tændte stearinlys på deres værelse.
examples.translation: They lit candles in their room.

examples.native: Tom taler aldrig om sine ekser.
examples.translation: Tom never talks about his exes.

rules.title: Relative clauses
rules.explanation: Som is a common relative marker; der can be a relative subject. Der also occurs in existence statements. Identify the role inside the relative clause.

examples.native: Alle æblerne, der falder ned, bliver spist af grisene.
examples.translation: All the apples that fall are eaten by the pigs.

examples.native: Alle æblerne er der.
examples.translation: All the apples are there.

examples.native: Hun arbejder som au pair.
examples.translation: She works as an au pair.

rules.title: Existence and place
rules.explanation: Der can mean there or support an existential construction. Her means here. A grammatical existence marker and a stressed location are not always interchangeable.

examples.native: Tom boede her hos os i tre måneder.
examples.translation: Tom lived here with us for three months.

examples.native: Jeg græder altid, når jeg ser det her billede.
examples.translation: I always cry when I see this picture.

examples.native: Der bor mange rige mennesker i det her kvarter.
examples.translation: Many rich people live in this neighborhood.

rules.title: Questions
rules.explanation: Direct questions often place the finite verb before the subject. An indirect question takes subordinate order. A question word specifies the information requested.

examples.native: Oh, hvor træet bævede!
examples.translation: Oh, how the Tree trembled!

examples.native: Kan du fortælle mig, hvordan man justerer lydstyrken?
examples.translation: Could you tell me how to adjust the volume?

examples.native: Og hvor kommer pengene fra?
examples.translation: And where is the money coming from?

rules.title: Infinitives
rules.explanation: At can mark an infinitive or introduce a finite complement clause. Distinguish at læse from at hun læser. Modals normally take an infinitive without at.

examples.native: Tom tog fra Boston til Chicago.
examples.translation: Tom went from Boston to Chicago.

examples.native: Toget ankom til Kyoto til tiden.
examples.translation: The train arrived in Kyoto on time.

examples.native: Brevet var adresseret til mig.
examples.translation: The letter was addressed to me.

rules.title: Comparison
rules.explanation: Comparatives commonly use end; equality uses forms such as lige så ... som. Bedre and større are irregular/common comparative forms.

examples.native: Det er koldere i år end sidste år.
examples.translation: It is colder this year than last year.

examples.native: I burde være mere forsigtige.
examples.translation: You guys should be more careful.

examples.native: Jeg er fire måneder yngre end dig.
examples.translation: I am four months younger than you.

rules.title: Prepositions
rules.explanation: Prepositions encode relations and belong to learned phrases. A location choice between i and på cannot always be predicted from English in/on.

examples.native: Jeg bor i Boston nu.
examples.translation: I live in Boston now.

examples.native: Tom arbejder på deltid.
examples.translation: Tom works part-time.

examples.native: Tom stod med ansigtet mod muren.
examples.translation: Tom stood facing the wall.

rules.title: Concession and inference
rules.explanation: Selvom introduces concession; alligevel means nevertheless; derfor supplies a consequence; måske limits certainty. Connectors carry argument meaning as well as clause structure.

examples.native: Tom er måske lun på dig.
examples.translation: Tom may have a crush on you.

examples.native: Politiet tror at Tom måske har forgiftet Mary.
examples.translation: The police think that Tom might've poisoned Mary.

examples.native: Det er måske en skør ide, men jeg synes at vi burde besøge Tom og Mary lige nu.
examples.translation: It may seem like a crazy idea, but I think we should go visit Tom and Mary right now.

passages.native: Jeg lærer et nyt sprog. Hver dag læser jeg en kort tekst og lytter til tydelige eksempler. Jeg skriver nyttige ord i en notesbog. Når jeg laver en fejl, ser jeg på reglen og prøver igen. Mit mål er at forstå mennesker og udtrykke mine tanker klart.
passages.translation: I am learning a new language. Each day, I read a short text and listen to clear examples. I write useful words in a notebook. When I make a mistake, I check the rule and try again. My goal is to understand people and express my ideas clearly.

grammarTerms: Noun
A word naming a person, thing or idea: student, book, freedom.
Verb
A word describing an action or state: read, know, be.
Subject
The participant linked to the main verb’s subject pattern. In The student reads a book, the student is the subject.
Object
A participant selected by a verb. In The student reads a book, a book is the direct object.
Agreement
One word changes to match another, for example an adjective matching a noun’s gender and number.
Case
A noun/pronoun form marking its relationship in a sentence. Cases can mark subjects, objects, possession or relations usually expressed by English prepositions.
Gender
A grammatical noun class. It does not always describe the sex of a person or any physical property.
Tense
A verb system that relates a situation to a time, often past or non-past.
Aspect
How a situation is viewed: unfolding, completed, habitual, experienced or in a resulting state.
Infinitive
A non-finite verb form often used for a dictionary entry or a complement. It does not by itself give the ordinary person/tense pattern.
Participle
A verb-derived form used in compound predicates or as a modifier; its exact function depends on the language and construction.
Clause
A unit organised around a predicate. One sentence can contain several clauses.
Register
Language choices suited to a situation: casual conversation, polite requests, academic writing or another context.
